qualtdict

License: MIT

Qualtrics is widely used to collect questionnaire and follow-up data, and the analyst’s work begins when the survey closes. Qualtrics describes a survey in a deeply nested JSON structure: questions, choices, matrix items, loops, embedded fields and scoring rules are spread across several API objects. The downloaded response file refers back to them only through identifiers like QID12_3_TEXT, and can contain hundreds of such columns covering question choices, matrix items, text-entry fields, Loop and Merge iterations, embedded data, scoring outputs and text-analysis sidecars. Before any analysis, every column has to be matched back to the metadata, renamed, labelled with its response options, and documented. Done by hand or in ad hoc scripts, that mapping is slow, error-prone, and hard for anyone else to check, especially for surveys with matrix, side-by-side or multi-select questions and repeated waves.

qualtdict makes that mapping explicit, readable and reproducible. From the Qualtrics metadata it builds a Variable Dictionary: a flat table with one row per exported response column, showing the question, item, response level and label it belongs to, plus a generated variable name. The dictionary is easy to inspect and validate, and it doubles as a codebook you can review with collaborators or publish alongside the data.

Applying the dictionary to downloaded responses attaches that structure to the data itself. Every column is renamed to its variable name; choice columns carry their response options as value labels, and text and numeric columns carry the question text as a variable label. You can tell what each column is just by looking at it, so the response data are analysis-ready from the first glimpse().

qualtRics handles the Qualtrics API; qualtdict handles everything between the raw export and your analysis. It is not a replacement downloader for qualtRics, and not a general survey-cleaning framework.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("lyh970817/qualtdict")

qualtdict does not need Java. The SystemRequirements field of its DESCRIPTION mentions Java only because the suggested openNLP package needs it for POS-tag filtering, which the Semantic Names in qualtdict do not use.

Credentials

dict_generate() and survey_fetch_labelled() read your survey from Qualtrics, so they need Qualtrics API credentials. Your institution must allow API access, and it must be enabled for your account; the person who manages your Qualtrics account can give you your API token and base URL. Store them once with qualtrics_api_credentials(), which qualtdict re-exports from qualtRics:

library(qualtdict)

qualtrics_api_credentials(
  api_key = "<YOUR-QUALTRICS_API_KEY>",
  base_url = "<YOUR-QUALTRICS_BASE_URL>",
  install = TRUE
)

The rest of the functions work on objects you already have and need no credentials.

A Variable Dictionary for your survey

Pass the survey ID to dict_generate():

survey_id <- "SV_XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX"

dict <- dict_generate(survey_id, variable_name = "question_name")

The rest of this README uses glad_example, a small example bundled with the package: the metadata of a subset of the GLAD Study sign-up survey (four demographic questions, the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 blocks, embedded data and scoring variables) with synthetic responses. glad_example$dictionary is exactly what dict_generate() returns for that survey.

library(qualtdict)

dict <- glad_example$dictionary
dict
#> # A tibble: 97 × 14

#>    <chr>              <chr>      <chr>   <chr>         <chr>         <chr>

Every column of the dictionary, with its type:

dplyr::glimpse(dict)

#> $ variable_name      <chr> "DEM.AGE.1.0", "DEM.COR.1.0", "DEM.COR.1.0", "DEM.C…
#> $ block              <chr> "Demographics", "Demographics", "Demographics", "De…

#> $ level              <chr> NA, "1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "0", "1", "1", "1", "1…
#> $ label              <chr> NA, "England", "Scotland", "Wales", "Northern Irela…

#> $ selector           <chr> "SL", "DL", "DL", "DL", "DL", "DL", "SAVR", "SAVR",…
#> $ sub_selector       <chr> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, "TX", "TX", "TX", "TX", "TX…
#> $ content_type       <chr> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…

The columns that identify a row are:

  • response_column_id: the column name in the downloaded Qualtrics response file, such as QID1147_5_TEXT. This is how the dictionary is matched to your data.
  • row_source: what the column comes from: a survey question, an embedded_data field, a scoring variable, or a text_analysis sidecar.
  • qid: the Qualtrics question the column belongs to. One question can produce many columns, such as one per matrix item or per ticked choice.
  • question_name: the question name you set in the Qualtrics survey editor.
  • variable_name: the name the column gets in your labelled data, unique and safe for export.

The other columns describe the content: the Survey Block, question text, item text, response level and label, and the Qualtrics question type. A column with response options takes one row per option. The first PHQ-9 item, “Little interest or pleasure in doing things”, is one response column with four levels:

dict[
  dict$variable_name == "PHQ.DEP.1.0",
  c("response_column_id", "variable_name", "level", "label")
]
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   response_column_id variable_name level label                  
#>   <chr>              <chr>         <chr> <chr>                  
#> 1 QID127303424_1     PHQ.DEP.1.0   0     Not at all             
#> 2 QID127303424_1     PHQ.DEP.1.0   1     Several days           
#> 3 QID127303424_1     PHQ.DEP.1.0   2     More than half the days
#> 4 QID127303424_1     PHQ.DEP.1.0   3     Nearly every day

Embedded data fields and scoring variables appear alongside the questions:

dict[
  dict$row_source != "question",
  c("response_column_id", "row_source", "variable_name", "question")
]
#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#>   response_column_id row_source    variable_name     question                   
#>   <chr>              <chr>         <chr>             <chr>                      
#> 1 Age                embedded_data Age               Embedded Data: Age         
#> 2 sex                embedded_data sex               Embedded Data: sex         
#> 3 PHQRaw             embedded_data PHQRaw            Embedded Data: PHQRaw      
#> 4 CurrentDepression  embedded_data CurrentDepression Embedded Data: CurrentDepr…
#> 5 GADRaw             embedded_data GADRaw            Embedded Data: GADRaw      
#> 6 CurrentGAD         embedded_data CurrentGAD        Embedded Data: CurrentGAD  
#> 7 SC_5gvP3Yxax8TWHcN scoring       GAD_7             Scoring Variable: GAD-7    
#> 8 SC_3rtKxr7Lzd9OHhX scoring       PHQ_9             Scoring Variable: PHQ-9

Check the dictionary

dict_validate() reports Validation Findings: dictionary rows worth a second look before you analyse the data.

findings <- dict_validate(dict)$validation_findings
findings[, c(
  "severity", "response_column_id", "original_candidate", "variable_name",
  "reason"
)]
#> # A tibble: 23 × 5
#>    severity   response_column_id original_candidate variable_name reason   
#>    <chr>      <chr>              <chr>              <chr>         <chr>    
#>  1 suggestive QID1147_2          DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.1 duplicate
#>  2 suggestive QID1147_3          DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.2 duplicate
#>  3 suggestive QID1147_4          DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.3 duplicate
#>  4 suggestive QID1147_6          DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.4 duplicate
#>  5 suggestive QID1147_5          DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.5 duplicate
#>  6 suggestive QID1147_5_TEXT     DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.6 duplicate
#>  7 suggestive QID1147_-999       DEM.EDU.1.0        DEM.EDU.1.0.7 duplicate
#>  8 suggestive QID127303424_2     PHQ.DEP.1.0        PHQ.DEP.1.0.1 duplicate
#>  9 suggestive QID127303424_3     PHQ.DEP.1.0        PHQ.DEP.1.0.2 duplicate
#> 10 suggestive QID127303424_4     PHQ.DEP.1.0        PHQ.DEP.1.0.3 duplicate
#> # ℹ 13 more rows

All findings here are suggestive: they report variable names that qualtdict repaired. The items of the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 matrices and the choices of the multi-select qualifications question share one Question Name, so their names are numbered to keep them unique, and the hyphen in the scoring variable names PHQ-9 and GAD-7 is not safe in an export variable name, so they become PHQ_9 and GAD_7.

A definite finding, such as two choices sharing one response code, would mean the column cannot be labelled reliably. dict_assert_valid() raises an error for such level-label findings, and survey_fetch_labelled() runs it before downloading anything.

Labelled survey data

survey_fetch_labelled() downloads the responses through qualtRics and applies the dictionary:

survey_dat <- survey_fetch_labelled(dict)

For the example survey, that call returns glad_example$labelled_survey_data:

survey_dat <- glad_example$labelled_survey_data
dim(survey_dat)
#> [1] 20 43
head(survey_dat[, c(
  "externalDataReference", "DEM.AGE.1.0", "DEM.SEX.1.0", "PHQ.DEP.1.0",
  "HEAD", "PHQRaw", "PHQ_9"
)])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   externalDataReference DEM.AGE.1.0 DEM.SEX.1.0 PHQ.DEP.1.0  HEAD PHQRaw PHQ_9
#>   <chr>                       <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 example-001                    34           0           3     0     16    16
#> 2 example-002                    53           0           1     3     14    14
#> 3 example-003                    63           1           0     1     13    13
#> 4 example-004                    37           0           1     3     12    12
#> 5 example-005                    68           0           3     3     15    15
#> 6 example-006                    70           0           3     3     14    14

Columns are named by variable_name. Choice columns carry their response options as value labels, and text and numeric columns carry the question text as a variable label:

attr(survey_dat$PHQ.DEP.1.0, "labels")
#>              Not at all            Several days More than half the days 
#>                       0                       1                       2 
#>        Nearly every day 
#>                       3
attr(survey_dat$DEM.AGE.1.0, "label")
#> [1] "How old are you now?"

so tools that read labels, such as sjlabelled, can use them directly:

table(sjlabelled::as_label(survey_dat$DEM.SEX.1.0))
#> 
#>   Male Female 
#>     11      9

survey_export_findings() lists dictionary columns that were missing from the download. For the example there are none:

survey_export_findings(survey_dat)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 5
#> # ℹ 5 variables: finding <chr>, response_column_id <chr>, qid <chr>,
#> #   variable_name <chr>, reason <chr>

One block at a time

dict_split_blocks() and survey_split_blocks() split the dictionary and the data by Survey Block. Embedded data fields and scoring variables are not assigned to a block by default, so they are kept under "..unassigned".

dict_blocks <- dict_split_blocks(dict)
names(dict_blocks)
#> [1] "..unassigned" "Demographics" "GAD7"         "PHQ9"
unique(dict_blocks$GAD7[, c("response_column_id", "variable_name", "item")])
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   response_column_id variable_name item                                         
#>   <chr>              <chr>         <chr>                                        
#> 1 QID127303430_1     HEAD          Feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge         
#> 2 QID127303430_2     HEAD.1        Not being able to stop or control worrying   
#> 3 QID127303430_3     HEAD.2        Worrying too much about different things     
#> 4 QID127303430_4     HEAD.3        Trouble relaxing                             
#> 5 QID127303430_5     HEAD.4        Being so restless that it is hard to sit sti…
#> 6 QID127303430_6     HEAD.5        Becoming easily annoyed or irritable         
#> 7 QID127303430_7     HEAD.6        Feeling afraid as if something awful might h…
#> 8 QID127303448       Q5            <NA>

survey_blocks <- survey_split_blocks(survey_dat)
names(survey_blocks$GAD7)
#>  [1] "externalDataReference" "startDate"             "endDate"              
#>  [4] "HEAD"                  "HEAD.1"                "HEAD.2"               
#>  [7] "HEAD.3"                "HEAD.4"                "HEAD.5"               
#> [10] "HEAD.6"                "Q5"

Semantic Names

If the Question Names in your survey are not good analysis names, ask for Semantic Names, generated from the question text. Here block_pattern turns each Survey Block name into a prefix:

block_pattern <- function(block) {
  substring(block, 1, 3)
}

dict <- dict_generate(
  survey_id,
  variable_name = "semantic_name",
  block_pattern = block_pattern,
  block_sep = "."
)

Semantic Names are a readable convenience, not stable identifiers: they can change with the survey text or the package version. They need the suggested packages slowraker, SnowballC, stringi and tidyr.

How To Cite

If qualtdict contributes to published work, please cite it. The citation for the installed version is returned by citation().

citation("qualtdict")
